Question: What's the use of async controller actions in C#/.NET?
Answer: —Jan, can you explain what initiating an asynchronous operation really means? Well, it means using a controller action in C#/.NET for operations that take an unacceptably long time to complete. —Such as? Things like querying a database, reading or writing files, making network requests, or doing complex calculations or data processing. —Why do I need to async such tasks? Well, if you don’t, in other words, if they’re done synchronously, you would cause the current thread to wait until they’re finished. —Is that bad? Bad is not the right word, although it can be. I’d say wasteful. —Ok, how does it work? An async operation is initiated that consists of two steps: a thread is used to initiate the task, but because the action takes time, the thread is freed for other tasks; once the initiated task is completed, a thread is re-employed to finish the remainder of the task. See a diagram here: —That is not very clear, although I get the main idea. Could you elaborate? Sure. Let’s see a more detailed one: When the await keyword is used, it says “start this operation, and then free up the current thread to do other work instead of waiting for this operation to finish”. —What’s an example of ‘this operation’? How is ‘this operation’ done now that we freed up the thread? Won’t it need a thread to be finished? An example is fetching data from the database. Now the responsibility of the task has been passed to the database to do its job, so our application thread is available again. We free the thread, so some other tasks can use it. —Ok, why is freeing up the current thread a good thing? Well, then the server can handle a higher number of concurrent requests without exhausting the available thread pool. Particularly important in scenarios with high traffic or long-running operations. —So, it allows my application to handle more requests and do other work while waiting for the database operation to complete? Exactly. It improves the overall responsiveness and scalability of your application. —Right. Can you give me a code example? Of course: As you can see, Index is an async controller action that fetches a list of employees from a database. —I see async in its declaration on line 15. Yeah, and await on 17 calling _context.Employees.ToListAsync(), a potentially long-running operation (because it queries a database). —Ok, so what does await do? It tells the .NET runtime to “pause” the Index() method and return control to its caller. Now the current thread is freed up to do other work. —And what happens after the database operation is completed? Once the database operation is complete, the .NET runtime schedules the remainder of the Index() method to continue executing. —Correct me if I’m wrong: when the operation is complete, the .NET runtime is notified to schedule the remainder of the async method (the code after the await keyword) to run on a thread from the available thread pool. Yes. But it doesn’t have to be the same thread that was started initially. It can be any thread. —Interesting. So in your code example, what is the remainder of the async method? In our example, when the result of _context.Employees.ToListAsync() is available, it is passed along to the View() method to generate the HTTP response. —Thanks, that makes sense now. You’re welcome.

Question: What language would you love to see replacing JavaScript for the web?
Answer: So far, there have been various attempts in this direction. WASM is the most disruptive of these. WASM is a binary instruction format designed to be portable and safe. Imagine a universal translator for code - it takes code written in various languages and compiles it into a format that can run in a web browser. Using WASM, websites run more complex applications, and they load faster too; we also have more options and flexibility in how we build web apps. In the context of WASM, I’ve been using C# and I’m satisfied. Performance is good and the experience is enjoyable.

Question: Can anyone learn to write beautiful code or is it a skill that only comes with experience?
Answer: Ah, I see. You're wondering whether some can write elegant code because their minds are wired in a certain way. The so-called hereditary advantages argument. I've met a lot of very attractive people who obviously had undergone plastic surgery. They often show me the ‘before’ photos. Politely speaking, the ‘before’ photos are nothing they should hang on walls… See where I'm going? Some things are predetermined (by randomness!) and if you've been dealt a good hand, well, then don't squander it. Those of us who were not so lucky, can opt for ‘plastic surgery’. I wasn't born a genius, although if I went all the way back to 1000 years ago or so, I'd discover I'm related to some famous polymath whose contributions have changed the world. So, I can improve my mind, at least. My point is: usually, if not always, it's not possible to be so gifted as to write elegant programs with very little effort. Unlike looks, brains are more forgiving and enjoy better plasticity. This is the good news. The bad news is, not every one knows about this, and even if they did (like probably you now), their neuro-linguistic mental models (after Bandler and Grinder) and self-efficacy (after Bandura) are not enhanced enough to give them the kind of sustained motivation that is needed to improve programming elegance via practice. In other words, most people are content with writing rubbish code, even though they could change and improve. It's the same logic in other spheres of life. The principle of ‘least cognitive effort’ is being misused or rather, abused, because the person is suffering from a mental model confusion. It's like wearing a hat that makes one lazy, mediocre and happy with status quo. Achievement motivation occurs as soon as one changes one's mental models. Even seeing others adopt great mental models helps one improve. The undisputed boxing world champion Bivol said in an interview: “I want to train hard so I can carve my name in boxing history.” That sort of mental model then provides the fuel for sustained motivation to achieve his stated goal. Most people don't even know there are mental models… And that's why the average programmer writes programs that are, in polite terms, not elegant at all, and worse, doesn't care about changing or improving: ‘don't fix it if ain't broke.’ You know.

Question: How do adults deal with adult bullies?
Answer: Answer # 600 It depends. Here on Quora there are plenty of bullies, for example. Since we won't have to meet in person, I block and mute anyone who rubs me the wrong way, and that's all that is needed. Then I focus on writing my answers and communicating with sane people. For those, too, ignore them (if rational) and move on, as you need to focus on your good life, not on some pointless conflict with a loser. The worse bully is the one you have no way to avoid. It can be a parent, a sibling, a neighbor, a teacher or classmates, a ‘friend’, a relative, a friend of a friend, etc. Each of these cases requires their own specialized defensive and protective measures. And it depends on the severity, frequency and the type of bullying. So, it's hard to generalize here. But if I had to, I'd say: try to distance yourself from the bully instead of direct conflict first. Ignoring won't help, and they will only become bolder. And the abuse would become more serious. Distancing is possible in only some of these cases. But if possible, it's best to make an evasive move, to waste bully's efforts to engage you. If it's a boss, change the job. If it's a friend, unfriend them. When distancing is not possible or realistic, the only way out is through, if you catch my drift. Make yourself strong in every aspect of your life, while you're being bullied. This is a sign that you have been perceived as a soft mark. So work on yourself, strengthen all your weaknesses, and when the time is right, strike back at the bully when they least expect it. Note that the most effective retaliation is psychological, indirect, invisible, if possible. Direct conflict at the physical level is mostly pointless. Movies teach you the wrong concepts. Will Smith slapping Rock is an example of people thinking physical altercation is a solution. It is not. If you engage in a physical, open and direct confrontation, you will end up right where you started. The problem has not been solved. A more effective way is show of strength without needing to exercise it. Twenty years ago when I was a younger man, I lived in China and in order to avoid loneliness, I would go to the bars (I don't drink) that were frequented by foreigners. I made a lot of friends. But sometimes, narcissists or bullies can't see you happy and they will pick on you. I politely told him to enjoy the night, relax, etc, but he took my conflict avoidance as weakness. He said: “let's go outside and settle this, man to man, we fight.” He was drunk and overconfident. I didn't even know what I had done to make him this angry. When I asked him, he said:” you know it. Don't pretend you don't”. And kept telling me to go out for a fight outside. (Inside there were security guards). The pest became annoying enough so I said to him: give me a minute (but I could have knocked him out myself easily, only I wanted to go Sunzi art-of-war on him). I went to the second floor where I had a dozen friends. One of them, a very tall, heavy-weight Cuban boxer, a chess buddy of mine. I told him let's go downstairs to chase some pest away. We went downstairs and towards the bully. When he saw me approach with my Cuban friend, his soul seemed to escape his body and he looked scared and defeated. I told him: ‘let's go out, shall we? I have gotten in a physical altercation as well, but that was totally unexpected: some crazy guy jumped me, and I had to break his nose in order to end it. Both Java and C# took inspiration from C and its cousin C++ (in the sense that wanted to improve upon them or they were Stackelberg followers.). Question: Considering that learning and understanding Haskell is harder than most of the other languages, what will learning Haskell give you in return, and will it pay off?
Answer: TOC Prelude Since questions like these are asked by people new to programming or at least, new to Haskell, I have a dilemma: If I write about what ‘Haskell gave me in return’, the answer would be useless if it was not understood. However, if I write something simple, something everyone could understand, then it would not reflect the exact truth of how Haskell made me a better programmer. I’m gonna with go simple, since at the very least, it will give a glimpse of what’s possible. One language to rule them all Let’s say you will never use Haskell in production. That may be because companies and jobs have already been (historically) tied to Algol-Simula-Lisp descendants. Programming culture inertia is difficult to completely overcome. But almost every language you will need to learn, new and old, have features that can be traced back to Haskell. Old languages constantly introduce new ‘functional’ capabilities that have existed in Haskell for decades. If you learn Haskell for fun and intelligence, the upside is, many features that are specifically implemented in any given language are a general recipe already present in Haskell. So learning the specific features in a new language you need to learn in two weeks (on the job) would be a walk in park, if you already know Haskell. Haskell also introduces the right kind of discipline and way of thinking in your programming style. Because of how Haskell does things, you’ll be tempted to write elegant Haskell-like code in your existing/day-job language. Haskell will teach you how to become a 10x programmer. And you do need to aspire to become a 10x programmer because, you don’t want to end up like this, as eloquently put by Erik Dietrich: This serves as important perspective for understanding why it’s common to find people with titles like “super-duper-senior-principal-fellow-architect-awesome-dude,” who make a lot of money and perhaps even wield a lot of authority but aren’t very good at what they do. The not-hard hard One thing most people coming to Haskell don’t realize is that Haskell depends on you. You can make it as hard as possible or as easy as possible. It’s a language that adapts to your level. For most routine stuff that you need to do, Haskell is pretty straight-forward and concise and easy to grok. But before you reach that level, you need to overcome the Haskell barrier. That barrier is not difficult to overcome, per se. It’s just different and requires a different kind of thinking than you’re used to. Do you need to be a mathematician to write Haskell? Of course, not. (But you can, if you were, too); however, Haskell exposes the links between programming and mathematics, and if you’re intellectually curious (you should be!), then you’ll find that this mathematical inclination will actually make writing and maintaining code easier—over the long run. As a simple example, you’ll probably see something called ‘fold’ in Haskell. Now that may appear ‘scary’ to someone who has forgotten their high school math, but mathematics, if properly taught, is actually quite intuitive. To do this, to get to manipulate those arguments, I’ve had to open the box, to unfold the box, you see? Now, what is the reverse of unfold? Is it fold? Indeed it is. Answer: I don’t think you understand ADHD. It’s not a disease. To cure. It’s merely neuro-divergence. The same way some people are left-handed. (I am). It’s unfortunate that the last word in the acronym stands for disorder. Given a second chance, I’d still choose to have ADH because the advantages far outweigh any so-called disadvantages. There’s a misconception being spread that ADH’s have ‘executive function’ failure; in other words, we can’t get stuff done. That’s not true. Well, not entirely true. If the thing is worth doing, we get it done better and faster than anyone else. The trick is to persuade ourselves that this thing is actually worth doing. That worth depends on too many factors, most of which are emergent. I think the ADH type prefers to do only specific kinds of things, to the exclusion of other things that they find soul-erasing. Ask me if I enjoy doing laundry? Or ‘give a speech’? No way. But I could write computer programs all day long. Hence I think it’s safe to claim that an ADH is likely good at a certain category of tasks, and exceptionally good at that. This comes at the cost of not being able to do what a neuro-normal person is able to accomplish. There are trade-offs.
